title: Partition, 1947
hookLine: India and Pakistan divide, millions are displaced and many killed on all sides

lines: AN OLD IRON KEY IN A DRAWER.
SURE SHE'D BE BACK IN A FEW WEEKS.
THE SAME KEY ON BOTH SIDES.
cards: A key. An old iron house key, kept in a drawer in Lahore, or Delhi, or Amritsar, or Dhaka. The family that keeps it hasn't seen the door it opens for generations.
The grandmother who carried it out locked the house behind her, sure she'd be back in a few weeks, once things calmed down. Families on both sides of a new border keep keys like this.
Hindu families, Sikh families, Muslim families. The same drawer, the same key, the same door they never opened again. Today: Partition.

teach.h: A LINE DRAWN IN A HURRY.
teach.b: When British rule in India ended, the land was divided into two states, India and Pakistan, with Pakistan itself in two wings, west and east.

A British commission drew the line in a hurry, through the provinces of Punjab and Bengal, through farms and villages and families. Some people learned which country they lived in only after independence had already come.
Then came the leaving. Muslims moving toward Pakistan. Hindus and Sikhs moving toward India.
On foot, in carts, on overcrowded trains.

And then the killing, done by people of every community to people of every community, neighbors turned against neighbors. Women suffered terribly. Accounts tell of trains that arrived carrying only the dead.
An honest telling says it plainly: cruelty on all sides, and grief on all sides. And there's the other thread.

The oral histories gathered since include people who hid a neighbor of another faith in a grain store, walked a family to safety, refused to give up a name. Hindus sheltering Muslims. Muslims sheltering Sikhs.
The Qur'an sets the weight of one life in a single sentence. In Pickthall's words: "whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind."
And at any loss, Muslims say the words of surah al-Baqarah: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." That summer, some had nothing else left to say. Grief on every side.

how: Families in Pakistan, India and Bangladesh pass down Partition memories, and Muslims, like their neighbors, remember those who died with prayers and with the words of Qur'an 2:156 said at any loss.

games.q: years later, someone asks you to tell the story of Partition honestly. what must the telling include?
o: only what was done to your own community.
cruelty on all sides, grief on all sides, and the neighbors who hid neighbors.
only the new borders, not the people.
games.why: the killing was done by people of every community to people of every community, and the oral histories also keep those who saved a life.

practice: Bring to mind the families who left their homes that summer, Muslim, Hindu, Sikh, Christian and others: the ones who arrived and the ones who didn't, the ones who hid a neighbor, the ones still holding the key.
Don't sort them into sides; just hold them, all together.
If you pray, you can pray for all who were uprooted and say the words Muslims say at a loss, we are Allah's, and unto Him we are returning; if not, just remember them as you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Partition. The division of British India into India and Pakistan, a leaving and a killing that left grief in every community. Today's word.

orig.note: Urdu: division, the everyday word families use for Partition (in Hindi, बँटवारा).

carryVoice: Your line: grief on every side. And on every side, someone who hid a neighbor. Gently, until tomorrow.
